name: Paris
title: Holidays in Paris
intro: Eiffel Tower picnics, carousels and Disneyland down the line, all a train ride from London. Here's what Paris is like with the family and when to go.
facts_note: The EU is bringing in new entry checks, so check the rules on GOV.UK before you book.
when_to_go: Late spring and September are the sweet spot, with long light evenings and parks at their best. Summer is busy at the big sights but the city itself empties in August. December brings Christmas markets and lights.

things.name: Eiffel Tower
things.blurb: Book lift tickets ahead, or picnic on the Champ de Mars underneath for free.

things.name: Jardin du Luxembourg
things.blurb: Toy sailing boats on the pond, pony rides and a great playground.

things.name: Disneyland Paris
things.blurb: About 40 minutes on the RER train. Worth two days if you're going.

things.name: Cité des Sciences
things.blurb: Hands-on science with a big play area just for young children.

things.name: Seine boat trip
things.blurb: See the sights from the river without little legs getting tired.

things.name: Jardin d'Acclimatation
things.blurb: An old-fashioned amusement park with rides, animals and water play.

faqs.question: Is Paris good for a family holiday?
faqs.answer: Yes. The parks, carousels and museums suit all ages, and you can arrive by Eurostar with no airport in sight. The metro has a lot of stairs, so pack light.

faqs.question: How many nights do you need?
faqs.answer: Three to five nights covers the city, or add two more for Disneyland Paris.

faqs.question: Do UK families need a visa?
faqs.answer: No, British passport holders can visit for up to 90 days in any 180 without a visa. New EU entry checks are being brought in, so check GOV.UK before you travel.

faqs.question: Is it better to go by train or plane?
faqs.answer: The Eurostar from London St Pancras takes about two and a half hours to the middle of Paris, so for most families in the south of England it's quicker door to door.
